title_en: Ferrero S.p.A. v. Mengtesha (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. and Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Marketing Co., Ltd. — dispute over unfair competition
ruling_gist_en: 1. The "well-known goods" referred to in the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China refer to goods that have certain market popularity within China and are known to the relevant public. For goods that are already well-known internationally, the protection of their unique name, packaging, and decoration still requires that they be known to the relevant public within China. Therefore, in determining whether goods are well-known, factors such as the sales duration, sales region, sales volume, and target customers of the goods in China, the duration, intensity, and geographic scope of any publicity, and the circumstances of protection as well-known goods shall be comprehensively assessed. It is also not excluded that the foreign fame of the goods may be appropriately considered.

full_text_en:
Ferrero S.p.A. v. Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. and Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Marketing Co., Ltd. — dispute over unfair competition

[Ruling Summary]

1. A well-known commodity as referred to in the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the PRC is a commodity that has a certain degree of market popularity within the territory of China and is known to the relevant public. For commodities that are already well-known internationally, the protection of their distinctive names, packaging, and decoration in China must still be based on the necessity that they are known to the relevant public within the territory of China. Therefore, in determining a well-known commodity, comprehensive consideration shall be given to factors such as the sales time, sales area, sales volume, and target customers of the commodity within China, the duration, intensity, and geographical scope of any publicity conducted for it, and the circumstances of its protection as a well-known commodity. The fact that the commodity is well-known abroad may also be appropriately taken into account.

2. Packaging, such as containers used to hold or protect a commodity, as well as the decoration constituted by the text, patterns, colors, and their arrangements attached to the commodity or its packaging, shall, when capable of distinguishing the source of the commodity, constitute distinctive packaging and decoration protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the PRC.

3. In the design of commodity packaging and decoration, different business operators may learn from and draw upon each other's designs. However, they shall not engage in comprehensive imitation of another's distinctive packaging and decoration that has the significance of identifying the source of the commodity, to an extent sufficient to cause market confusion or misidentification. Otherwise, such conduct constitutes unfair competition.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2006) Min San Ti Zi No. 3

Petitioner for Retrial (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 9 Zhenxing Road, Zhangjiagang City, Jiangsu Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Cai Xinghua, Chairperson of the Board of Directors of the Company.

Authorized Agent: Huang Bin, Manager of the Administrative Department of the Company.

Authorized Agent: Zhou Mian, Attorney from Beijing Tonghaolin Law Firm.

Respondent for Retrial (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Ferrero S.p.A., domiciled at Piazzale Pietro Ferrero 1, 12051 Alba, Province of Cuneo, Republic of Italy.

Legal Representatives: Sergio Testa and Massimo Gaidano.

Authorized Agents: Bai Tao, Attorney from Beijing Jun He Law Firm; Teng Yue, Attorney from Beijing Jun He Law Firm.

Defendant at First Instance: Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Marketing Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 12E, Building B, Kaixuanmen Mansion, Nanjing Road, Hexi District, Tianjin, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Guo Yongxin, Manager of the Company.

In the case of the dispute over unfair competition between Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Montesa Company) and Ferrero S.p.A. (hereinafter referred to as Ferrero Company) and Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Marketing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhengyuan Company), Montesa Company, dissatisfied with the Civil Judgment (2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36 rendered by the Tianjin High People's Court, filed a petition with this Court for a retrial. Upon review, this Court found that the petitioner's application met the conditions for case docketing for retrial as stipulated in Article 179, Paragraph 1, Item (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and on May 10, 2006, ordered the retrial of this case in accordance with the Civil Ruling (2006) Min San Jian Zi No. 4. On January 10, 2007, this Court lawfully constituted a collegial panel composed of Kong Xiangjun, Deputy Chief Judge of the Third Civil Adjudication Tribunal, serving as Presiding Judge, Judge Wang Yongchang, and Acting Judge Xi Zhonglin, and held a public hearing of this case, with Court Clerk Wang Xin serving as the recorder. Huang Bin and Zhou Mian, the authorized agents of Montesa Company, and Bai Tao and Teng Yue, the authorized agents of Ferrero Company, appeared in court for the proceedings. Zhenyuan Company, having been properly summoned by this Court, failed to appear without justifiable cause, and this Court proceeded with the trial in absentia. The trial of this case is now concluded.

Ferrero Company filed a lawsuit with the Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court, alleging: Since 1984, Ferrero Company has sold chocolate products in the Chinese market through China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation, and its products currently hold a significant market share in China. The plaintiff's products are well-known commodities not only worldwide but also within China, known to virtually everyone. Over the years, these products have maintained a distinctive packaging and decoration that encompasses multiple intellectual property rights of the plaintiff, including trademarks, design patents, and copyrights. This packaging and decoration is original and represents a comprehensive embodiment of the plaintiff's intellectual property. The distinctive packaging and decoration used by Ferrero Company for its chocolate products consist of: (1) Golden, spherical paper packaging; (2) A label attached to the golden paper ball packaging, featuring an oval gold border and bearing the plaintiff's "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark, as decoration; (3) Each piece of chocolate in the golden paper ball packaging is provided with a brown paper base as decoration; (4) Hard plastic packaging boxes of various shapes, the covers of which are transparent to reveal the golden paper ball inner packaging; (5) Use of the plaintiff's composite trademark featuring product patterns as decoration, from which extend ribbon-shaped patterns in red and gold colors. The golden paper ball packaging and the oval, gold-bordered label affixed thereto effectively constitute the three-dimensional trademark of the plaintiff's product, enjoying a very high level of recognition among consumers. Any consumer seeing chocolate products with the aforementioned packaging and decoration would identify them as the plaintiff's products. Defendant Montesa Company has for many years been imitating the plaintiff's products, unauthorizedly using packaging and decoration that are identical or similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration of the plaintiff's well-known commodity, thereby misleading consumers and causing confusion. Furthermore, whenever the plaintiff launches a new product or seasonal product, it is immediately imitated by Montesa Company. Even new products launched in Europe are imitated before entering the Chinese market. The aforementioned actions of Montesa Company and the conduct of Defendant Zhengyuan Company in selling the imitative products have had a serious adverse impact on the plaintiff's production and sales, infringed upon the legitimate rights and interests of the broad consumer base, and caused significant economic losses to the plaintiff. Ferrero Company requested the court to order Montesa Company to cease production and sale, and Zhengyuan Company to cease selling chocolate products that use any one or any combination of the packaging and decoration elements unique to Ferrero Company's chocolate products, or any chocolate products similar to the above-mentioned packaging and decoration of Ferrero Company that are sufficient to cause consumer misidentification. Further requests included Montesa Company issuing an apology, eliminating the adverse effects, bearing the litigation costs, and compensating the plaintiff for economic losses in the amount of RMB 3,000,000.

Montesa Company responded in its defense: The plaintiff's product in question is not known to the relevant public within the Chinese domestic market, and there is no evidence proving its sales volume and market share within China. On the contrary, the "Jinsha" chocolate products produced by Montesa Company enjoy a very high reputation among consumers in China, having won multiple awards, and are well-known commodities. The packaging and decoration for which the plaintiff seeks protection in its complaint are the common packaging and decoration used for similar chocolate products both domestically and internationally, lacking originality and specificity. Furthermore, this packaging and decoration are dictated by the functional nature of the product and cannot be considered distinctive packaging and decoration. The packaging and decoration used for the Jinsha chocolate produced by Montesa Company were developed through the cooperation of its own employees and professional designers from Zhangjiagang Arts and Crafts Printing Factory, undergoing several improvements before finalization, and were not imitations of existing packaging and decoration of others. An ordinary consumer, exercising ordinary care when making a purchase, would not confuse the chocolate products produced by the plaintiff and the defendant. The plaintiff claimed that its product packaging encompasses multiple intellectual property rights such as trademarks, designs, and copyrights, but did not specify which of these rights were specifically infringed upon by the packaging and decoration of the allegedly infringing product. The subject matter of the plaintiff's lawsuit is vague. Therefore, the plaintiff's lawsuit lacks factual and legal basis, and the court is requested to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

Defendant Zhengyuan Company did not submit a defense or provide any evidence.

The Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court found the following facts at first instance: In 1986, Ferrero Company registered the "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark in China. Its "FERRERO ROCHER" series of chocolate products (hereinafter referred to as FERRERO ROCHER chocolate) entered the Chinese market before 1988 through China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation via consignment sales. The overall appearance and arrangement of its products have remained largely unchanged from those currently sold, with only minor changes in details. Starting in 1993, Ferrero Company gradually intensified its print media and outdoor advertising for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate in China, focusing on regions including Guangdong, Shanghai, and Beijing. It subsequently set up specialty counters in various large and medium-sized cities for sales and enhanced product visibility through sponsorships of commercial and sports events. In June 2000, its "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark was included in the National Key Trademark Protection List by the State Administration for Industry and Commerce.

Montesa Company is a Sino-foreign equity joint venture established in December 1991 by Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory and Belgian Fetadel Co., Ltd., engaged in the production and sale of various chocolate products. Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory was a collective enterprise established in December 1989, dealing in products such as malted milk and chocolate. In June 1993, upon approval by the System Reform Committee of Jiangsu Province, Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Corporation was established with Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory as its main body, later renamed Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. Montesa Company is one of the closely affiliated enterprises under Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd., and its Chinese investor subsequently changed to Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. On April 23, 1990, Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory applied to register the word mark "JINSHA," which was approved by the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce in April 1991. Ferrero Company petitioned the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce in 1994 to cancel this trademark but was unsuccessful. Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory was a state-collective joint enterprise without legal personality established in March 1989, and it obtained legal personality in March 1992, primarily dealing in malted milk and chocolate products. Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory was one of its associated enterprises, and simultaneously, Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory was a subsidiary company under Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. Governmental certifications for Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory's qualifications consistently included annotations referring to Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory. Before 1993, honors awarded for chocolate using the "JINSHA" trademark (hereinafter referred to as JINSHA chocolate) were granted to Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory. From the second half of 1992 onwards, the promotion and sale of JINSHA chocolate were branded under Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory or Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. preceding Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory.

Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory began producing JINSHA chocolate in 1990. The packaging and decoration of this product are essentially identical to those of the allegedly infringing chocolate produced and sold by Montesa Company since 2002, and are relatively similar to those used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. This product was recognized as a municipal-level new product by the Zhangjiagang Economic Commission in 1990. It won a silver award at the Second Beijing International Expo in 1991, the gold award for Outstanding New Products in Jiangsu Province's Seventh Light Industry Sector, and the Second Prize in Jiangsu Province's Third Light Industry Art Design Exhibition and Evaluation. In 1992, it received the title of Suzhou's Second Outstanding New Product. During this period, JINSHA chocolate was also promoted and sold as a product of Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory. In 1998, JINSHA chocolate was selected by the China Bakery and Confectionery Industry Association as one of the recommended products representing excellent chocolate brands in the Chinese market. In 2000 and 2001, it was consecutively rated as National Quality Standard-Compliant Food by the China National Food Industry Association, and received the China Well-Known Food Brand Reputation Award in 2000. In 2000, it was recognized as a Key Protected Product of Jiangsu Province by the Jiangsu Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision. In 2001, it won a gold award at the Western Famous Brand Product Trade Fair. In 2004, it was rated as a China Famous Brand Product and designated as a national exemption inspection product. The "JINSHA" trademark was recognized as a Suzhou well-known trademark and a Jiangsu Province famous trademark in 2001. Through extensive promotion of JINSHA chocolate by Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Factory and Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. since 1992, its fame gradually increased. Concurrent with receiving the aforementioned honors, JINSHA chocolate ranked prominently in nationwide food market surveys and chain store sales statistics and monitoring rankings published by entities such as the China National Commercial Information Center or the National Chain Store Supermarket Information Office, as reported in the "China Food News," from 1997 to 2002. FERRERO ROCHER chocolate did not appear in these statistical rankings.

In 2002, Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory transferred the "JINSHA" trademark to Montesa Company. (The application was filed on November 25, 2002, and the assignment was approved by the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce on April 21, 2004.) Montesa Company then began producing and selling JINSHA chocolate. Zhengyuan Company was the distributor of JINSHA chocolate produced by Montesa Company in Tianjin City. In January 2003, Ferrero Company, notarized by the Tianjin Public Notary Office, purchased the allegedly infringing products from Zhengyuan Company in Hedong District, Tianjin.

After trial at first instance, the Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court held: A well-known commodity is one that has a certain degree of popularity in the market and is known to the relevant public. Given its distinct territorial characteristics, the degree of a commodity's fame abroad does not represent its fame within the territory of China. Whether a commodity is well-known and the degree of its fame shall be determined based on the specific circumstances of the market in which it exists. As early as the 1970s, the practice of wrapping spherical chocolate in gold foil paper and using transparent plastic outer packaging to reveal the inner packaging of the chocolate was already used by other chocolate producers and was not unique to FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. This packaging constitutes common packaging and should not be protected. However, the decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, which Ferrero Company had used before entering the domestic market in 1988, possesses distinctive features capable of identifying and beautifying the commodity and distinguishing its source, thus constituting its distinctive decoration. Although the JINSHA chocolate produced and sold by Montesa Company continues the decoration used by Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory, the earliest use of this decoration for JINSHA chocolate was in 1990, which is later than that of Ferrero Company. The other evidence provided by Montesa Company is insufficient to negate the distinctiveness of the decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate products. Therefore, items (2), (4), and (5) of the decoration for which Ferrero Company sought protection in its complaint shall be recognized as distinctive to FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. The production and sale of the allegedly infringing JINSHA chocolate products by Montesa Company represented the marketing strategy of Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. for the operation of this product by its affiliated companies. Montesa Company's succession in producing the product inheriting from Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory and Shanghai Foreign Trade Shen Gang Foodstuff Farm was continuous. The development process of JINSHA chocolate cannot be fragmented due to adjustments among production entities within the group; rather, the overall continuity of the product should serve as the benchmark for examination and evaluation. Since its launch by Zhangjiagang First Dairy Factory in 1990, JINSHA chocolate has consistently used a decoration that is identical to that of the allegedly infringing chocolate and simultaneously similar to that of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Subsequently, through extensive promotion by the various production entities led by Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd., JINSHA chocolate achieved a leading market share among chocolate products and won numerous accolades from national government departments and related associations, becoming a highly popular commodity in China. Under the circumstances where both the plaintiff's and the defendant's chocolate commodities are well-known commodities in China, the chronological order of their fame and the relative levels of their fame should serve as specific factors for determining whether an ordinary consumer would mistake the defendant's product for the plaintiff's product. Analyzing the timing of their fame, JINSHA chocolate produced by Montesa Company had, by the mid-1990s, gradually developed from a product recognized by local governments and consumers into a nationally well-known commodity with a high market share, and was rated as a China Famous Brand Product in 2004. For a period after entering the domestic market and until before 1993, FERRERO ROCHER chocolate was sold only in a few locations such as duty-free shops in certain cities and airports, thus having a more distant connection from the lives of ordinary consumers. It did not achieve recognition during that period. After 1993, FERRERO ROCHER chocolate primarily used Guangdong, Shanghai, and Beijing as its main markets for promotion and sales, gradually expanding its sales scope from these three core areas. In recent years, it has become a well-known commodity in China, but its recognition occurred later than that of JINSHA chocolate produced by Montesa Company. Regarding the relative fame of the two chocolate commodities, the consecutive years of market sales share rankings provided by Montesa Company indicated that consumers held a high degree of recognition for JINSHA chocolate, which frequently appeared at the top of the rankings. FERRERO ROCHER chocolate never appeared in these rankings, sufficiently indicating that the fame of JINSHA chocolate was significantly higher than that of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Due to the high and long-lasting fame of JINSHA chocolate, it has developed stronger distinguishing features relative to other brands of chocolate, and the distinctiveness of the product's appearance has continuously increased. Under these circumstances, consumers would not mistake Montesa Company's JINSHA chocolate for Ferrero Company's FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Furthermore, during the decade-long coexistence, promotion, and sale of the chocolate products of Montesa Company and Ferrero Company in the domestic market, both parties placed great emphasis on their respective product trademarks and places of origin. The different requirements regarding product quality, price, taste, and consumer demographics resulted in each party having its own consumer base. Since Ferrero Company's "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark and Montesa Company's "JINSHA" trademark are both prominently placed on the product packaging, consumers can distinguish them based on differences in the chocolate's trademark and manufacturer, purchasing the products they need. The similar decoration can no longer become an obstacle to consumer choice. Therefore, although the decoration of the two products is similar, it is insufficient to cause consumers to misidentify or confuse the two products. In summary, the packaging and decoration used by Montesa Company in producing JINSHA chocolate do not constitute unfair competition against Ferrero Company, and Zhengyuan Company's act of selling JINSHA chocolate also does not constitute infringement.

On February 7, 2005, the Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court rendered its first-instance judgment: Dismissing all claims of Ferrero Company against Montesa Company and Zhengyuan Company.

Ferrero Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, filed an appeal on the following grounds: 1. The court of first instance confused the TRESOR DORE chocolate produced by Montresor Company with the confectionery products bearing the "Jinsha" trademark, and erroneously determined the time when FERRERO ROCHER chocolate became well-known within China and the fact that the allegedly infringing product, TRESOR DORE chocolate, became well-known within China. 2. The court of first instance disregarded the evidence of the international renown of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate and erroneously concluded that the degree of renown of a product abroad does not extend to China. In reality, both the Trademark Office and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce recognized that FERRERO ROCHER chocolate had extensive renown as early as the 1980s, which is closely related to the degree of renown it achieved internationally. 3. The court of first instance erroneously denied the distinctiveness of certain packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, ignored the basic principles of comparison in isolation, overall comparison, and comparison of main parts, and violated the fundamental principles of relevant laws and regulations, leading to the erroneous conclusion that despite finding the packaging and trade dress used on TRESOR DORE chocolate to be similar to those used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, there was no likelihood of confusion. 4. The court of first instance erroneously interpreted the concept of the relevant public, incorrectly excluding consumers who had access to goods in duty-free shops from the relevant public, and further stratified the relevant public based on the price of the goods and their different consumption levels. 5. The court of first instance also failed to recognize Montresor Company's acts in bad faith as alleged by Ferrero Company, such as the preemptive registration of the "Jinsha" trademark and the false labeling of "since 1968" on the product labels. Therefore, Ferrero Company requested the court of second instance to reverse the judgment of first instance, uphold its claims, and order Montresor Company to bear all litigation costs of this case.

Montresor Company responded and argued: The allegedly infringing product is the Jinsha chocolate, and the packaging and trade dress of the allegedly infringing product are precisely those used on Jinsha chocolate. The "TRESOR DORE" trademark was registered in 2003, and Montresor Company's use of the "TRESOR DORE" trademark in combination with "Jinsha" on its own products did not change the source of the products. The mere fact that FERRERO ROCHER chocolate was sold in China through consignment clearly established that it could not have been well-known in the domestic market in the 1990s. The court of first instance correctly considered factors such as the duration and scope of sales, market share, and advertising to conclude that FERRERO ROCHER chocolate only gradually became a well-known product among the relevant public in recent years, with the time of becoming well-known being later than that of Montresor Company. The packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, apart from the trademark portions, lack distinctiveness. The court of first instance's findings were largely correct, except for its erroneous identification of items 2, 4, and 5 of Ferrero Company's claims as distinctive. Ferrero Company misinterpreted the concept of the relevant public and the standards for assessment. The judgment of first instance was correct in its findings of fact, application of law, and substantive ruling. Therefore, Montresor Company requested the appeal be dismissed and the judgment of first instance be affirmed.

Upon trial of the appeal, the Tianjin High People's Court confirmed most of the facts found by the court of first instance. It additionally found the following: Ferrero Company was established in Italy in 1946; its FERRERO ROCHER chocolate was launched on the market in 1982, and advertisements were placed on television, in newspapers, and in magazines in multiple Asian countries and regions. In the Taiwan region and the Hong Kong market of China, FERRERO ROCHER chocolate was named "Jinsha" chocolate, and the "Jinsha" trademark was registered in the Taiwan region in June 1990 and in the Hong Kong region in 1993. In February 1984, FERRERO ROCHER chocolate entered the domestic market through consignment by China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation, and was primarily sold in duty-free shops and airport stores, as permitted by policies at the time, continuing until before 1993. In October 1986, Ferrero Company registered in China the series trademarks "FERRERO ROCHER" and the design (elliptical lace pattern) and combinations thereof, and used them on chocolate products sold within China. The main features of the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are: 1. Each ball-shaped chocolate is wrapped in gold-colored paper; 2. An oval gold-rimmed label printed with the "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark is affixed to the gold ball-shaped wrapping as trade dress; 3. Each gold ball-shaped chocolate has a coffee-colored paper base as trade dress; 4. Several shapes of transparent plastic packaging are used to display the gold ball-shaped inner packaging; 5. An oval gold-rimmed pattern is used on the transparent plastic packaging as trade dress, with the product image and trademark inside the oval, and a gold-red ribbon pattern extends from the trademark. The three-dimensional packaging for 8-piece, 16-piece, 24-piece, and 30-piece FERRERO ROCHER chocolate products was filed for registration as three-dimensional trademarks with the World Intellectual Property Organization in 1984. The administrative authorities for industry and commerce in Guangdong, Hebei, and other places in China repeatedly investigated and dealt with acts of imitating the packaging and trade dress of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Montresor Company produces and sells Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate products. Apart from replacing the mark with the combined trademark "Jinsha TRESOR DORE", it continues to use the packaging and trade dress that were used on Jinsha chocolate products by Zhangjiagang City Dairy No. 1 Factory. In July 2003, the "TRESOR DORE" trademark was registered with the approval of the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, with the registrant being Jiangsu Liangfeng Food Group Co., Ltd. The packaging and trade dress used on the Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate products produced by Montresor Company and distributed by Zhengyuan Company are essentially the same as the main features of the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate.

The Tianjin High People's Court held in its trial of the appeal that the well-known goods referred to in China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law are goods that have been sold in a specific market and are known to the relevant public. The assessment of the well-known status of goods should be determined by comprehensively evaluating their renown in specific markets both domestically and internationally, and cannot be understood as referring only to goods well-known within China. Ferrero Company, as an internationally renowned enterprise specializing in the production of chocolate confectioneries, is a well-known fact in the industry. The FERRERO ROCHER chocolate it produces was already known to the relevant public in the chocolate market and had a high degree of renown before entering the domestic market for sale in 1984. Since its public sale in China began in 1984, the unique packaging and trade dress of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, as a whole, had significant visual features and effects in the Chinese market at that time. Thereafter, through long-term sales in the Chinese market, this product became known to the relevant public and should be recognized as a well-known product. The packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate constitute an overall design that conveys specific meanings and forms a unique form of packaging and trade dress. Montresor Company's Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate uses packaging and trade dress that are essentially identical to those of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, and Montresor Company cannot prove that it independently designed or used them earlier. Therefore, it was determined that Montresor Company had, without authorization, used the unique packaging and trade dress of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. In accordance with the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics standards, a well-known product should be the result of honest business operations; legally, business achievements obtained through the use of unfair competition means cannot be used as the basis for evaluating a product's renown. Montresor Company, by without authorization using the unique packaging and trade dress of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate to produce and sell Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate, directly affected the sales and renown of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Therefore, if Ferrero Company's claims were to be dismissed on the grounds that the market renown of Montresor Company's Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate in China is currently higher than that of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, this would effectively perpetuate the consequences of the unfair competition in this case. The trial of this case, in accordance with the provisions of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China on the application of law in civil relations involving foreign elements, should apply the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China. Additionally, as both China and the Republic of Italy are member states of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, where the laws of China differ from the Convention, the provisions of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property shall apply. Pursuant to Article 10bis of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, when applying Article 5(2) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China in this case, the application should not be limited to the general circumstances enumerated by the law. In this case, the conduct of Montresor Company should be found to constitute unfair competition that causes confusion with respect to Ferrero Company's goods and commercial activities and should be prohibited by law. Therefore, the trial of this case should, in accordance with the purposes and principles of China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law and relevant international conventions, uphold good faith and fair competition in commercial activities. The application of law in the judgment of first instance was improper, and the handling was not fair. The main grounds of appeal of the appellant, Ferrero Company, are well-founded and are to be upheld.

On January 9, 2006, the Tianjin High People's Court, in accordance with Article 130, Article 153(1)(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 1, 2, and 5(2) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China, and applying Article 10bis and 10ter of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, rendered the following judgment: 1. Revoke the judgment of first instance; 2. Montresor Company shall immediately cease using the infringing packaging and trade dress of the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate; 3. Montresor Company shall compensate Ferrero Company in the amount of RMB 700,000, payable within fifteen days after this judgment takes effect; 4. Order Zhengyuan Company to immediately cease selling Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate using the infringing packaging and trade dress; 5. Dismiss Ferrero Company's other claims. The first instance case acceptance fee of RMB 25,010 shall be borne by Montresor Company in the amount of RMB 20,000 and by Ferrero Company in the amount of RMB 5,010. The second instance case acceptance fee of RMB 25,010 shall be borne by Montresor Company in the amount of RMB 20,000 and by Ferrero Company in the amount of RMB 5,010.

Montresor Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of second instance, filed an application for retrial with this Court, arguing that the judgment of second instance contained errors in findings of fact, legal basis, and substantive ruling. The main reasons were: 1. The expansive interpretation of "specific market" by the court of second instance does not comply with the provisions of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, and moreover, that Convention does not specify how to determine well-known goods. The international renown of Ferrero Company's products cannot logically be extrapolated to their renown in the domestic market. 2. The market share of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate is lower than that of Jinsha chocolate. In the absence of contrary evidence, the court of second instance erroneously overturned the finding of fact from the first instance that the time when FERRERO ROCHER chocolate became well-known was later than that of Montresor Company's Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate. 3. The packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are generic packaging and trade dress in the international chocolate industry and lack distinctiveness. Finding this packaging and trade dress to be distinctive would allow Ferrero Company to exclusively and monopolistically use generic packaging and trade dress of the chocolate industry, thereby monopolizing the domestic ball-shaped chocolate market. Furthermore, in a case where Ferrero Company accused Taiwan Dachang Trading Co., Ltd. of violating the Fair Trade Act, the Fair Trade Commission of the Executive Yuan of the Taiwan Region found that the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate lack distinctiveness. The packaging and trade dress for the Jinsha chocolate products used by Montresor Company were independently developed and designed by commissioned professionals. Montresor Company has been using this packaging and trade dress for 15 years since 1990, and this type of packaging and trade dress is now adopted by many chocolate production enterprises domestically and abroad. Ferrero Company has never, in accordance with the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, claimed before a people's court or an administrative authority that Montresor Company imitated the packaging and trade dress of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate; now, the assertion of such rights has no value for protection. 4. As a high-end confectionery, chocolate consumers primarily rely on trademark identification when purchasing and do not identify by packaging or trade dress; similar packaging and trade dress would not cause consumer confusion. 5. The judgment of second instance exceeded the scope of the parties' claims. Ferrero Company only sued for infringement of the packaging and trade dress used on Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates T3, T8, T16, T24 (referring to 3-piece, 8-piece, 16-piece, and 24-piece packages respectively), but the judgment of second instance ordered Montresor Company to immediately cease using the packaging and trade dress of the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate, which illegally included seven other products produced by Montresor Company, such as T12, T36, T42, T45, and the 4-piece, 8-piece, 16-piece paper box packages, violating the principle of "no trial without complaint" in civil procedure. Therefore, Montresor Company requested the revocation of the judgment of second instance, the upholding of the judgment of first instance, and an order that Ferrero Company bear all litigation costs of this case.

Ferrero Company responded, arguing that the judgment of second instance had clear findings of fact and correct application of law, and that Montresor Company's grounds for retrial lacked factual and legal basis. The main reasons were: 1. The court of second instance correctly found the well-known status of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate and its entry into the Chinese market in 1984. 2. Montresor Company could not prove that the packaging and trade dress in question were independently designed by itself or used earlier. 3. The court of second instance correctly found that Montresor Company, in violation of the principle of good faith and recognized moral standards, imitated the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, and therefore could not recognize its product as a well-known product; it thus did not assess the time when Montresor Company's product became well-known. At the same time, the court of second instance refuted the court of first instance's approach of comparing the renown of the two products. Therefore, the judgment of second instance fundamentally upheld the standard of good faith established by China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law. 4. The packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate have distinctive features that distinguish them from other products and are unique. This packaging and trade dress, through shape, size, pattern, color, arrangement, combination, and placement, comprehensively form the unique identification of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. An average consumer, upon seeing this distinctive packaging and trade dress, can identify and associate it with FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. 5. Since the packaging and trade dress used on the Jinsha chocolate produced by Zhangjiagang City Dairy No. 1 Factory first emerged in the 1990s, they have undergone many changes. Currently, the Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate produced by Montresor Company has significantly differed from the packaging and trade dress used at the time of its initial launch and is very similar to the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, enough to cause consumer confusion and mistaken identification. Even if Montresor Company has used the current packaging and trade dress for a long time, this does not affect Ferrero Company's application for protection of its related rights. 6. The judicial decision of the court in the Taiwan Region concerning the packaging and trade dress of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate cannot serve as a reference basis for the trial of this case. 7. The order in the judgment of second instance that Montresor Company cease using the infringing packaging and trade dress of the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate was precisely the packaging and trade dress that Ferrero Company sought to protect in its claims in the first instance; it did not exceed the scope of the claims. Therefore, Ferrero Company requested the dismissal of Montresor Company's application for retrial and the upholding of the judgment of second instance.

Within the time limit for adducing evidence, the applicant for retrial, Montresor Company, submitted the following new evidence to this Court: 1. A letter from the China Bakery & Confectionery Industry Association certifying that the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are generic packaging and trade dress. 2. Review decisions by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce rejecting Ferrero Company's applications for territorial extension of protection for its three three-dimensional trademarks, being Shangpingzi [2006] No. 3190, Shangpingzi [2006] No. 3191, and Shangpingzi [2006] No. 3192. These prove that Ferrero Company's applications for three-dimensional trademarks for the packaging and trade dress of the products in question have been rejected. 3. Decisions by the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office on requests for invalidation of three design patents of Ferrero Company, being No. 6606, No. 6607, and No. 6913. These prove that Ferrero Company's design patents for the packaging and trade dress of the products in question have been declared invalid. 4. A ruling from the Supreme Administrative Court of the Taiwan Region, proving that the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate lack distinctiveness. 5. Three chocolate products produced and sold outside the Chinese market that use packaging and trade dress similar to those used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, namely Capitol, Capricci, and Anio chocolates. These prove that the packaging and trade dress used on FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are generic packaging and trade dress. 6. Three trademark opposition review rulings by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, being Shangpingzi [2006] No. 4134, Shangpingzi [2006] No. 4135, and Shangpingzi [2006] No. 4136. These prove that, although the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board found in prior cases that Ferrero Company's "FERRERO ROCHER and device" trademark had a relatively high degree of renown, it was insufficient to establish that this trademark had a relatively high degree of renown in China before November 27, 1995.

Within the time limit for adducing evidence, the retrial respondent Ferrero SPA submitted to this Court the following new evidence: 1. Judgments of foreign courts finding that imitation of the packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate constitutes infringement. Evidence that courts in France, Germany, the Czech Republic, Turkey, and other countries have determined that the packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are distinctive and have afforded protection. 2. A judgment of the Tel Aviv District Court in Israel finding that the Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate product produced by Montesa constitutes an infringing product. 3. Judgments of the Shilin District Court and the High Court in the Taiwan region of China. Evidence that the infringement litigation in the Taiwan region concerning the packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate mentioned by Montesa has not yet been finally adjudicated. 4. The "Legal Opinion on Trademark" issued by the China Trademark Appraisal Center. Evidence that the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are not generic but are distinctive. 5. Documents evidencing the registration in the Taiwan region of a three-dimensional trademark for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Evidence that the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are distinctive. 6. A market research report by Beijing Huatong Minglue Information Consulting Co., Ltd. Evidence that the brand awareness and market penetration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are higher than those of the Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate product. 7. Survey data from Shanghai Nielsen Market Research Co., Ltd. regarding FERRERO ROCHER chocolate and Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate. Evidence that the sales volume and market share of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate in major cities nationwide in 2004 and 2005 were higher than those of Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate. 8. An advertisement published in the fourth issue of 1990 of "CAAC" magazine. Evidence that FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, with packaging and decoration consistent with that at issue, was advertised and sold in China in 1990 under the name "Jinsha" chocolate. 9. Physical samples of other chocolate products of Ferrero that were not yet sold in China, and other well-known foreign chocolate products, which Montesa had imitated. Evidence of Montesa's subjective bad faith in the imitation.

This Court finds further upon retrial: The facts found by the courts of first and second instance are substantially correct.

This Court additionally finds: The packaging and decoration of the allegedly infringing Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate are as follows: Each piece of Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate is spherical and wrapped in gold foil; the top of each gold spherical wrapper is affixed with an oval gold-edge label bearing the "Jinsha TRESOR DORE" trademark; each gold spherical chocolate is accompanied by a bowl-shaped coffee-colored paper base with a smooth, wrinkle-free bottom and wavy pleats on the sides; the outer packaging is transparent plastic wrap or a plastic box; the center of the outer packaging uses an oval gold-edge pattern, incorporating a product image and the Jinsha TRESOR DORE trademark, from which a red-gold ribbon extends. The above features are similar in overall impression and main components to the packaging and decoration claimed by Ferrero SPA for protection in its lawsuit.

Opinion of the Court

This case primarily concerns the following contentious issues: whether FERRERO ROCHER chocolate is a prior well-known commodity; whether the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are distinctive packaging and decoration; and whether the use by Montesa of the packaging and decoration for its Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate constitutes unfair competition.

I. Whether FERRERO ROCHER chocolate is a prior well-known commodity

Based on evidence such as the consignment contract and the confirmation of the consignment contract signed between China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation and Ferrero SPA, the court of second instance correctly found that FERRERO ROCHER chocolate has been sold within Chinese territory since 1984. The "well-known commodity" as referred to in the Anti-Unfair Competition Law means a commodity that has a certain degree of market reputation within Chinese territory and is known to the relevant public. For goods that are internationally well-known, the protection afforded by Chinese law to their distinctive names, packaging, and decoration still requires that they be known to the relevant public within Chinese territory. The claimed reputation of a commodity or service usually arises from production, sale, or other business activities conducted within Chinese territory. To determine whether a commodity is well-known, a comprehensive assessment shall be made considering factors such as the time, region, volume, and targets of sales, the duration, extent, and geographic scope of any promotion, and the history of protection as a well-known commodity. The possibility of appropriately considering the factor of being well-known abroad is not excluded. The expression in the second instance judgment that "the evaluation of a commodity's reputation should be made comprehensively based on its reputation in specific markets both domestically and internationally, and cannot be construed as referring only to commodities well-known within Chinese territory" was inappropriate. However, based on the time of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate's entry into the Chinese market, its sales situation, and the various promotional activities conducted by Ferrero SPA, finding it to be a well-known commodity with relatively high reputation in the relevant market within Chinese territory was correct. The retrial applicant's claim that FERRERO ROCHER chocolate became well-known in the Chinese domestic market later than Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate cannot be sustained.

II. Whether the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are distinctive

Packaging, such as containers for holding or protecting a commodity, and the decoration composed of text, graphics, colors, and their arrangements affixed to the commodity or its packaging, fall within the scope of distinctive packaging and decoration protected by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law when they are capable of distinguishing the source of the commodity. The packaging and decoration that Ferrero SPA seeks to protect for its FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are composed of a series of elements. A simple combination, such as wrapping a spherical chocolate in aluminum foil, using transparent plastic outer packaging, and displaying the inner packaging of the chocolate, would result in packaging and decoration that lack distinctive features to distinguish the source of the commodity and therefore would not be distinctive. Moreover, each element in such a combination is a generic packaging or decoration element in the food packaging industry and cannot be exclusively used. However, there is considerable choice in the arrangement of packaging materials, shapes, and colors, such as foil, paper bases, and plastic boxes. There is also great freedom in designing the size, pattern, and layout of trademark labels affixed to the packaging. Within the scope of freely designable elements, a unique arrangement of packaging and decoration elements that gives the packaging and decoration distinctive features to distinguish the source of the commodity may constitute distinctive packaging and decoration for the commodity. Because the constituent elements of the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are uniquely arranged in terms of text, graphics, colors, shapes, and sizes, forming a distinctive overall image unrelated to the functional aspects of the commodity, and through long-term use and extensive promotion, it is sufficient to lead the relevant public to associate the overall image of the said packaging and decoration with Ferrero SPA's FERRERO ROCHER chocolate product, thereby serving to identify the source of the commodity. Therefore, such packaging and decoration should be considered distinctive packaging and decoration protected under Article 5, Item (2) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The retrial applicant's arguments that finding the packaging and decoration at issue to be distinctive would result in Ferrero SPA's exclusive use of generic packaging and decoration in the chocolate industry, thereby monopolizing the domestic spherical chocolate market, among other reasons, cannot be sustained.

Furthermore, Ferrero SPA used the packaging and decoration for its FERRERO ROCHER chocolate earlier in time. Montesa's claim that the packaging and decoration it used were independently developed and designed lacks sufficient evidentiary support. The second instance judgment correctly found that Montesa used the distinctive packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate without authorization.

This lawsuit seeks to protect the overall design of the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, composed of elements such as text, graphics, colors, shapes, and sizes, by means of restraining acts of unfair competition. This protected overall image design is different from a three-dimensional mark (stereoscopic trademark) and does not affect the independent judgment of the relevant authorities on the registrability of such a three-dimensional mark. The decision of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce rejecting Ferrero SPA's application for territorial extension of a three-dimensional trademark, submitted by Montesa, is not directly related to this case and does not affect its disposition. The legal protection requirements for distinctive packaging and decoration of well-known commodities also differ from those for design patents. The decision of the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office regarding Ferrero SPA's design patent invalidation declaration request, submitted by Montesa, is also not directly related to determining whether the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate are distinctive. The ruling of the "Supreme Administrative Court" in the Taiwan region submitted by Montesa and the judgments of foreign courts submitted by Ferrero SPA are also not relevant to the relevant market in this case and cannot serve as the basis for fact-finding in this case.

III. Whether the relevant public is likely to be confused or mistaken between FERRERO ROCHER chocolate and Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate

Different business operators may learn from and draw upon each other's designs for commodity packaging and decoration, and make innovative designs based on them, thereby forming packaging and decoration that clearly distinguish their respective commodities. This practice is an inevitable requirement of market operation and competition. In this case, Montesa could fully utilize the generic elements in chocolate packaging and decoration design to freely create packaging and decoration that are clearly distinguishable from the prior distinctive packaging and decoration used by others. However, one must not engage in wholesale imitation of another's distinctive packaging and decoration that serves to identify the source of the commodity, to the extent that it is likely to cause market confusion or misidentification, as this would constitute unfair market competition. The "confusion or misidentification" stipulated in China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law refers to circumstances sufficient to cause the relevant public to misidentify the source of the commodity, including mistakenly believing that there is a specific relationship such as a licensing arrangement or affiliated enterprise relationship with the operator of the well-known commodity. In this case, because the overall image of the packaging and decoration used for FERRERO ROCHER chocolate has distinctive features that distinguish the source of the commodity, and the packaging and decoration used by Montesa on its chocolate products are visually very similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, even if there are differences in price, quality, taste, consumption level, and factors such as different manufacturer names and trademarks between the two products, the relevant public is still likely to mistakenly believe that Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate has some economic connection with FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. Accordingly, the retrial applicant's argument that the similar packaging and decoration in this case would not cause consumer confusion or misidentification cannot be sustained.

IV. Whether the second instance judgment exceeded the parties' claims and whether the amount of damages awarded was appropriate

During the first instance proceedings, Ferrero SPA specifically alleged that the T3, T8, T16, and T24 Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate products produced by Montesa used packaging and decoration similar to its distinctive packaging and decoration without authorization, causing consumer confusion and misidentification. Although Ferrero SPA did not explicitly enumerate the infringement claims regarding the seven other chocolate products produced by Montesa, namely T12, T36, T42, T45, and the paper-box packaged 4-piece, 8-piece, and 16-piece products, in its complaint, Ferrero SPA requested a judgment ordering Montesa to cease production and sale of any product that uses any one or a combination of the distinctive packaging and decoration elements of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, or any product with packaging and decoration similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate sufficient to cause consumer misidentification. The above-mentioned additional seven chocolate products produced by Montesa also all adopted packaging and decoration similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate. The second instance judgment ordering Montesa to immediately cease using the infringing packaging and decoration of the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate did not exceed Ferrero SPA's claims.

The distinctive packaging and decoration of a well-known commodity fall within the scope of commercial identifiers. The damages for the unfair competition act stipulated in Article 5, Item (2) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law may be determined by reference to the method for calculating damages for infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. Since Ferrero SPA failed to provide evidence to prove its economic losses caused by the unfair competition act in this case or the profits obtained by Montesa as a result thereof, the people's court, when determining the amount of damages, may, by reference to the provisions on statutory damages in the Trademark Law, award compensation not exceeding RMB 500,000 based on the circumstances of the infringement. Accordingly, the second instance court's order that Montesa pay Ferrero SPA RMB 700,000 in damages was without legal basis and should be corrected. This Court, taking into comprehensive consideration factors such as the reputation of FERRERO ROCHER chocolate, the duration and scale of Montesa's unfair competition acts, determines, in its discretion, that Montesa shall pay Ferrero SPA RMB 500,000 as compensation for economic losses.

Furthermore, what Ferrero SPA seeks to protect in this case is the distinctive packaging and decoration of a well-known commodity. Article 5, Item (2) of China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law already provides clear protection for this, and there is no inconsistency with the relevant provisions of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property. Since domestic law already has provisions that comply with the requirements of the Convention, there is no need to invoke the relevant provisions of the Convention. Therefore, the reasoning in the second instance judgment that "where there are differences between Chinese law and the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, the provisions of the Convention shall apply; in applying Article 5, Item (2) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law to this case, it should not be limited to the general circumstances enumerated in the law, and Montesa's conduct should be found to constitute unfair competition that causes confusion for Ferrero SPA's commodities and business activities" was inappropriate and should be corrected.

In summary, Montesa, in producing its Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate products, used packaging and decoration similar to the packaging and decoration of Ferrero SPA's FERRERO ROCHER chocolate without authorization, which is sufficient to cause the relevant public to be confused or mistaken about the source of the commodities, thus constituting an act of unfair competition. The reasoning in the second instance judgment was partially flawed, but its holdings that Montesa's conduct constituted unfair competition and ordering Montesa to immediately cease using the illegal packaging and decoration of the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate were not improper. For the purpose of clarifying the boundary between the distinctiveness of the overall image of the packaging and decoration protected under this case and the generic nature of certain constituent elements, as well as the boundary between this distinctive packaging and decoration and the relevant three-dimensional trademarks separately claimed by Ferrero SPA, and to more accurately define the scope of the unfair competition conduct in this case, appropriate adjustments are made to the relevant part of the main text of the second instance judgment. The determination of the damages amount in the second instance judgment was improper and shall be corrected. Pursuant to Article 5, Item (2) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 177, Paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, judgment is rendered as follows:

1. Uphold item 1 and item 5 of the Civil Judgment (2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36 of the Tianjin High People's Court;

2. Amend item 2 of the Civil Judgment (2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36 of the Tianjin High People's Court to: Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease the unfair competition act of using, on its Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate products involved in this case, packaging and decoration that are similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration used for FERRERO SPA's FERRERO ROCHER series chocolate products;

3. Amend item 3 of the Civil Judgment (2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36 of the Tianjin High People's Court to: Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. shall, within fifteen days after the service of this judgment, pay Italian company Ferrero SPA RMB 500,000 in compensation. In the event of late payment, interest on the debt for delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

4. Amend item 4 of the Civil Judgment (2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36 of the Tianjin High People's Court to: Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Xingxiao Co., Ltd. is hereby ordered to immediately cease selling the above-mentioned Jinsha TRESOR DORE series chocolate products.

The first instance case acceptance fee of RMB 25,010 shall be borne by Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 20,000 and by Italian company Ferrero SPA in the amount of RMB 5,010. The second instance case acceptance fee of RMB 25,010 shall be borne by Montesa (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 20,000 and by Italian company Ferrero SPA in the amount of RMB 5,010.

This judgment is final.
